hx_shade_height_field — 2D halcon_ext op

• Data kinds: image → image

• Call: fullseye.apply(img, "hx_shade_height_field", a=0.5, b=0.5) (the 2-D model is one image plus two scalar knobs a,b∈[0,1])

• HALCON equivalent: shade_height_field (the HALCON reference is a useful guide to its meaning and parameters)

*The figure is the actual output on a synthetic 128×128 input. Left: input, right: output. Point clouds are drawn as a top-down scatter (brightness = z), 1-D series as a line plot, volumes as the maximum-intensity projection along z, videos as the middle frame, complex images as magnitude; return values that are not pictures are shown as the values themselves.*

*The output is shown in a viridis-like pseudo-colour (dark purple = low, yellow = high) so that a field of quantities — distance, phase, orientation, depth — can be read.*

*The 4th column is a colour (H,W,3) input. This op handles colour without crossing channels (it does not convolve the colour channel as a third spatial axis).*

Usage

Render the height field v with Lambertian shading (normal × light). The light is at azimuth a and elevation b.

Treats v as a height field (gray value = height, pixel spacing 1), builds the normal n = (-gx, -gy, 1) / sqrt(gx^2 + gy^2 + 1) from (gy, gx) of np.gradient, clips from below at 0 the dot product n·l with parallel light of direction l = (cos(el)cos(az), cos(el)sin(az), sin(el)), normalises by min-max to [0,1] and returns it (Lambertian shading).

• a → light-source azimuth az = a*2*pi (lx = cos(az) is the column-direction component, ly = sin(az) the row-direction component).

• b → light-source elevation el = (0.2 + 0.7*b) * pi/2 (about 18° to 81°; 1 is close to directly overhead).

Caution: there is no height scale factor, and [0,1] values are differentiated over hundreds of pixels, so the gradients are tiny. As-is there is hardly any shading difference, but the final min-max normalisation makes it visible. Hence the absolute brightness of the output has no meaning, and a flat input gives 0 at every pixel. Meant for visually checking the unevenness of depth images or of a background surface estimated with hx_fit_surface2.

Blank frame (measured): feeding an image of uniform brightness gives an empty result — every pixel is background (0) — regardless of the brightness. Pure white and pure black behave alike; brightness by itself detects nothing.
